text: A few years ago,
I was speaking with a business leader who was frustrated.
He was always pitching new ideas to his team
on how they could work together better and faster.
But his team didn't seem to take up those ideas very often.
At the end of our conversation, he said something that stayed with me.
"I don't understand why they won't just change."
In my work as a consultant,
I've watched people ask their colleagues to change in a million different ways.
It's "I want you to change the way you write that report,"
It's "I want you to change the way you write that report,"
or "I want you to use these new inputs in your demand forecast."
Or sometimes, "I want you to meet with your manager more often."
They're different in detail, but they're the same in spirit.
It's people asking other people to do things differently.
Sometimes it works, and sometimes it doesn’t.
But why?
Why do some asks succeed
when other asks fail?
What's the secret to getting the people you work with to change?
After years of interacting with business leaders,
behavioral scientists, thousands of employees,
here's what I found.
There are two types of people who want their coworkers to change,
and I call them the dreamers and the detectives.
The dreamers mostly ask one question:
Why wouldn’t people do it?
Dreamers have a passionate belief
that the new way of doing things is smarter,
faster, fairer than the old way.
faster, fairer than the old way.
They think the benefits are self-evident,
and they struggle to comprehend that anyone else would see it differently.
But often, the dreamers don't get their wish.
People don't change
because there are too many barriers in their way.
The detectives ask a different question.
Not “Why wouldn’t people do it?”
but instead, “Why won’t people do it?”
Detectives don't get caught up in their own feelings
about why the new way of doing things is good or important.
about why the new way of doing things is good or important.
Instead, they investigate the frictions,
the disincentives that will prevent people from changing.
And consistently, it's the detectives who get better results.
Here's one example.
A hotel chain wanted its staff members
to use a more modern, sophisticated tool to set room prices,
one that relied more on automation and machine learning.
But through good investigation,
leaders learned that staff members were skeptical.
They weren't convinced that the new tool could improve
They weren't convinced that the new tool could improve
on their own pricing instincts.
So they pulled together the chain's most skilled,
experienced staff members
and put them into an early user group for the new tool
to signal to the organization
it really was valuable.
And it worked.
Before long, the vast majority of staff members
who had access to the tool were using it every week.
In your own life, I'm sure there are things
that you want other people to do differently.
As a detective,
you can ask, “Why won’t they do it?” in a few different ways.
Here's a simple one.
What knowledge and skills are people missing?
This question roots out gaps in the information
people have about the change
and gaps in their own ability to play their part.
If this is the barrier,
you need to give people the information and tools that they need.
Here's another variant.
What frictions will get in people's way?
Sometimes people feel they don't have the time
Sometimes people feel they don't have the time
or resources to do things differently.
Sometimes other people are quietly encouraging them
not to change at all.
In these cases, you have to remove the frictions,
provide time, provide resources,
have hard conversations with those other influential people.
One more for you to consider.
Why won't people want to change?
When people feel they don't gain anything by changing,
or worse,
when they feel that they have something to lose,
when they feel that they have something to lose,
we shouldn't be surprised when they don't change at all.
When this happens, you have to help people see things differently,
alleviate their unfounded fears
or show how you will personally help prevent the worst of them.
When you ask these questions, you learn a lot.
You learn that the person you're asking to run the new risk assessment
is the very same person who designed the old one.
To them, the change represents a loss of status.
To them, the change represents a loss of status.
You learn that your operations manager loves scheduling truck deliveries.
To them, the change to an automated system
represents the loss of a treasured creative activity.
And once you've learned, you can act.
As you get started, here are a few tips to keep in mind.
First, ask out loud.
It's good to imagine why people won't change,
but it's much better to sit them down in a meeting or over coffee
but it's much better to sit them down in a meeting or over coffee
and actually ask them.
Second, ask more than once.
Often you won't find the complex barriers to change,
like deep personal fears,
until you've addressed the simple ones,
like not having enough time.
Finally, never moralize.
When people aren't behaving the way you expect,
it's tempting to say that they're lazy or resistant,
but moralizing doesn’t help you get the thing that you want:
a successful, sustained change.
a successful, sustained change.
By the way, you can be a detective outside the workplace as well.
Maybe you want your sister to start using the family's shared calendar,
or an old friend to send more life updates.
The same principles apply.
So the next time you want someone to do something differently,
remember the magic question.
Don’t ask, “Why wouldn’t they do it?”
Ask instead, “Why won’t they do it?”
You'll be surprised how changing the question
You'll be surprised how changing the question
can change everything.
